Just finished this today and can highly recommend for those who may not have read it.

Set on the West coast (San Francisco maybe) in the 50s and 60s, the book follows the life of drinker and part-time gambler, Henry Chinaski, as he works at the Post Office over 15 years or so.

The book is set into four or five main parts, with relatively short chapters (some are less than half a page, some are maybe four or five pages). Most chapters are kind of "anecdotes", but they do add to the narrative and meld into one another seamlessly. These anecdotes don't always revolve around the Post Office, more around Hank's choices in life.

The writing is sincere and funny; this is only the second book in a while to make me laugh aloud. Bukowski isn't politically correct, neither is he degenerate with his writing. Also, it was written in 1970 and set just before then, so it's nice that the book is relatively modern, but nostalgic; good for Gen X'ers especially.

I'm actually a very slow reader, but I knocked this book off very quickly as the writing was straightforward and flowing and because I couldn't put it down. It's 160 pages.

For the red-pilled man, I can highly recommend this book. It's light, but the story resonates with the average man trying to make his way in the Western world (even now).
Book recommendation: Post Office - Charles Bukowski
